Senses.Explanation: The phrase describes picking up one item and putting down one item. In the Pang Yun–Yaoshan Weiyan exchange, Pang calls it not yet a good hand, while Yaoshan replies with the same phrase and says it is indeed a good hand. Dahui Zonggao applies it to endless worldly matters, and Juelang Daosheng says it is not yet the work of an accomplished hand. The evaluations remain context-specific rather than a single technical definition.

Senses.Explanation: To pick out and bring forward is a public, transitive action in these records: something is selected or taken up and put where others can hear, see, inspect, or receive it. Zhenjing Kewen brings Mazu's Sun-Face Buddha and Moon-Face Buddha wording forward again for his audience (日面佛，月面佛，一一為君重拈出). Duanqiao Miaolun says he must bring out one phrase so that what heaven and humanity have not heard or seen may be heard and seen (拈出一句子，使天上人間未聞者聞、未見者見). Gaofeng Yuanmiao brings an old doubt forward again from the beginning in a letter (今日重疑，不免從頭拈出), and Lu Hang asks that the cases of the various houses not be brought forward before requesting one direct phrase (諸家因緣，不勞拈出). The same verb governs presented objects. Pufeng Haidong tells an unnamed monk who claims to have a jewel, “try bringing it out and let us see” (試拈出看). Baichi Yuan says he will take a bright pearl from inside his robe and present it before the assembly (不免乘時拈出，對眾分付). Tian'an Sheng and Yongji Rong bring out incense for public offering. These are not two different headword senses: phrases, cases, doubts, jewels, pearls, and incense are different direct objects of one selecting-and-presenting action. Chan bends that action into a standard verb for putting inherited cases and a participant's claimed answer into the public exchange, while retaining its use for objects physically displayed and offered.

Senses.Explanation: To take up an inherited case, encounter, or saying and bring it before listeners for comment. The action belongs to the public handling of the record: the material is raised, quoted, appraised, or deliberately left without further comment. Wumen Huikai's publication notice calls his book “forty-eight cases taking up and presenting the encounters of buddhas and ancestral teachers” (拈提佛祖機緣四十八則). Jingfu says lineage descendants successively raised and voiced the inherited material and took it up for comment (舉唱之、拈提之); his editorial rules classify the collected material as masters' “statements of taking up and commenting” (諸師拈提語). Yuanwu Keqin uses the verb for a person moving within and bringing forward the upward hinge (向箇裏出沒，向箇裏拈提). Dahui Zonggao puts two opposed statements together “without further taking them up for comment” (更無拈提), leaving students to distinguish them. Yulin Tongxiu says few in the communities had taken up and commented on the old woman's burning-the-hut case (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者). Dagui Huaixiu appraises Baofu Congzhan's handling as having considerable house style, then says that under questioning it again dragged through mud and carried water (保福拈提，頗有宗風，及乎問著，又却拖泥帶水). The term is attested.

Senses.Explanation: To take up the mallet and raise the whisk names the exact named speaker’s visible handling of teaching-seat implements while presiding, questioning, or answering before an assembly. Yunmen Wenyan describes teachers in other quarters making this display and asking whether people understand, then proposes a reply and a blow. Xuansha Shibei uses the same visible act in his test of how one receives blind, deaf, and mute interlocutors; the blind person cannot see it. Pin Jixiang treats the display as something contemporary teachers take pride in. Baichi Yuanshuo says his own use has no other purpose than announcing who he is, while Huazang Anmin proposes a scriptural account of the usual gesture and is laughed out of that resting place by Yuanwu Keqin. An unnamed monk challenges Xuefeng Yicun over whether the display suits higher teaching, and Xuefeng answers by raising the whisk. The phrase identifies an institutional teaching-seat action and its public visibility. The following words and responses vary, so the entry assigns no single hidden message to every lift of mallet or whisk.

Senses.Explanation: Hold up a flower and smile is the compact case-name for the flower assembly, and later records keep it public by versifying, questioning, crediting, and openly criticizing it. Wuyi Yuanlai makes the phrase a verse heading. An unnamed monk asks Konggu Daocheng what the matter amounts to, and another asks Feiyin Tongrong who receives the bag and bowl after this single precedent. Baiyun Shouduan's verse questions whether the flower and smile can simply be accepted as the house style. The tradition also refuses a uniformly reverent reading. Juelang Daosheng connects the case with entrusting the treasury of the true teaching-eye to Kasyapa, while Puxian Yuansu says it still misses the measureless mechanism and Liang Dianhua's preface calls it the Buddha's first leak.

Senses.Explanation: Hold up a flower to show the assembly names the Buddha's public action in the flower case: the flower is raised before the gathered audience, Kasyapa smiles, and later masters repeatedly quote, criticize, reenact, or ask what could serve as its present counterpart. Wuyi Yuanlai says the Buddha's final flower-display and claim of a separate transmission look like a dream when inspected, then compares that inherited scene with his own circumstances. Feiyin Tongrong narrates the flower, Kasyapa's smile, and the entrusting of the teaching-eye treasury as the beginning of a transmitted succession reaching his present seat. Baojian Fada attacks the scene directly: the flower-display is empty self-pointing and Kasyapa's smile falls into a second moon. Wuming Huijing's verse retains the action as the Buddha's final line after other explanations. Baiyu Jingsi receives an unnamed monastic's explicit comparison between the Buddha's flower-display and the present abbot's guidance. These uses establish the public case-action without requiring a reverential verdict.

Senses.Explanation: The flower-lifting and smile scene names the paired actions attributed to the Buddha and Kashyapa; later masters quote, judge, and sometimes reject the scene’s inherited formulation. The flower-sermon scene: Shakyamuni Buddha holds up a flower before the Vulture Peak assembly, the assembly is at a loss, and Kashyapa smiles. The compact phrase joins two different actors' gestures; it does not say that one person both holds the flower and smiles. The recorded Buddha then entrusts Kashyapa with the treasury of the true teaching eye and a transmission outside teachings. Later masters challenge the scene. Yuelin Zongshan assigns thirty blows at the moment of the flower and smile. Dongshan Shouchu says people know the compact phrase but do not know the World-Honored One. Yulin Tongxiu calls it a single transmission and says it has made clear-eyed people laugh. Zhongfeng Mingben says that if the great affair were exhausted by such gestures, holding up the flower and smiling and cutting off an arm to settle the mind would be mere plays. Tianran Hanshi calls only this purport real and all other verbal teachings false, then immediately warns against making it a fixed reality. Zen defines the invoked Buddha and Kashyapa through this public scene, entrustment, and later examinations rather than through general hagiography.

Senses.Explanation: To take up incense is the ritual gesture that introduces the words or action attached to that incense in the particular ceremony. Konggu Daocheng takes up incense and names its recipient before saying it will be burned. Elsewhere an official, a disciple, or a named teacher takes it up before a question, dedication, lineage statement, or compact verdict. The gesture is stable; its actor, audience, recipient, and purpose are source-specific. It is therefore not defined as invariably public, dedicatory, or restricted to named teachers, and it remains distinct from subsequently burning the incense.

Senses.Explanation: Lamp after lamp continues first pictures one light kindling another without the light ending. At the Lantern Festival, one lamp lights hundreds and thousands and lamp after lamp continues; the physical lighting supplies the visible image. Shoushan Xingnian and later masters use that same image for the teaching reaching the present and for patriarch following patriarch. They then ask what, exactly, is continued or transmitted. Zen bends a chain of lit lamps into a public lineage claim, but does not erase the actual lamps from which the claim gets its force. Duplicate editions of Shoushan’s address are one encounter family, not two independent facts.

Senses.Explanation: 燈籠 is a lantern, the familiar light-holder of the monastery. Gulin picks it up in a verse; Yuanwu pairs it with the exposed pillar as an image of inertness; and Linji lists lantern and exposed pillar as stock visible objects. These rhetorical turns depend on the same ordinary object rather than a separate metaphysical entity.
